1: # Minimal translation from accepted NL0
2: 
3: Start with the accepted source map and specification. Read the supplied proof
4: and definitions where needed to choose faithful types. Other Yui documents,
5: library searches and individual background notes are available on demand;
6: there is no requirement to preload the entire skill or all note bodies.
7: 
8: 1. Preserve the accepted source and Audit A. Use a source revision only when an
9:    actual mathematical change or useful shared extraction requires it. Reusing
10:    unchanged acceptance runs integrity checks, not another model Audit A.
11: 2. Choose the mathematical representation, complete original H/E input types,
12:    N/P output types and useful local proof obligations. The controller copies
13:    source paragraphs and note locations. Mathlib is freely available; retain an
14:    M port only when useful, otherwise apply the library directly. Supply short
15:    `endpoint_correspondence` notes for every E and complete P (including all
16:    hypotheses), explaining direct or equivalent translation. Save partial interface drafts, revise
17:    those drafts, and use small Lean probes for uncertain types. Do not restart
18:    from an empty interface after an ordinary error.
19: 3. Type-check source correspondence, dependency boundaries and the complete
20:    interface, then obtain a separate independent semantic interface review.
21:    Normal full/translation entry dispatches no proof worker before its actual
22:    hash-bound receipt passes. Repair located failures with the interface author
23:    and have the same separate reviewer assess changed output. Final machine Audit B
24:    inherits that review only if the actual complete artifact preserves the freeze. The
25:    lower-level legacy mechanical freeze can record `PENDING_AUDIT_B`; it does
26:    not satisfy this normal-workflow pre-proof gate.
27: 4. Run local proof workers on frozen conditional obligations. Each gets its
28:    input statements, matched source paragraphs and own compact note index.
29:    Read a full note only if useful. No sibling proof bodies, other cases,
30:    developer history or additional personal skills are supplied.
31:    Use [Lean implementation safeguards](lean-writing.md) for library
32:    applications and conversions, including small type checks in preparation.
33:    Yui proof workers receive these requirements in their stage instructions.
34: 5. Attempt mechanical [assembly](assembly.md) and complete native inspection.
35:    Use the serial connection author only for real connection/library-discharge
36:    repair under unchanged E/P/definitions. Normal final Audit B is machine-only:
37:    inherit the actual pre-proof semantics after checking full endpoint types,
38:    defining header and complete closure. Only proof-valid interface drift opens
39:    B-final. Faithful drift is warning-qualified; a nonpass waits for the user's
40:    explicit delivery/recheck/translation-reset choice. Invalid proof is never
41:    semantically overridden.
42: 
43: ## Background notes are references, not extra ports
44: 
45: New contracts select `source.background_mode: node_local_reference`. Original
46: H/E/M/N/P entries remain unchanged; Audit A's verified supplement remains
47: hash-bound. Do not turn every note into a new M root, retype its entire library
48: signature, or require an extra theorem merely to restate it. The frozen
49: stage-one text's historical `background.effective` expansion is still supported
50: as `promoted_inputs` for old contracts; it is not the new translation default.
51: 
52: At the pre-freeze semantic review and final Audit B, notes are guidance, not library permissions. All proved results in
53: the pinned Mathlib environment are available without registration. Review every
54: external E and complete P against its actual Lean type using the concise author
55: correspondence explanation; independently check direct or equivalent meaning.
56: A new external assumption or stronger hypothesis still returns to the source
57: boundary. See [the complete Audit B standard](audit-b.md).
58: 
59: ## Work continuously, report genuine blockers
60: 
61: There is no ordinary `TASK_INCOMPLETE` reporting tool. While unfinished, keep
62: making concrete edits, queries or proof checks. Submit a completed artifact or
63: report a supported mathematical/source/input blocker. If a model turn ends
64: without either, the controller sends one short continuation instruction; it
65: does not demand a progress essay. State/usage recording is programmatic.
66: Proof workers follow [structured diagnosis and repair](proof-repair.md): report
67: actual packet obstructions. Progress counters are passive; no idle-turn count
68: cancels sibling work or authorizes interface changes.
69: 
70: Whole-case/stage execution, total tokens and calls are unlimited by default.
71: Each native check has the configured 180-second wall limit and finite Lean
72: heartbeat policy. Keep measuring usage and allow explicit
73: cancellation. Only a user-requested finite case deadline covers the entire
74: translation, including preparation, queue waiting, parallel proofs, assembly
75: and Audit B; later stages cannot reset that optional deadline. Preserve partial
76: results and report execution health separately from mathematical acceptance.

Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
value.conclusion: With the stipulated Euclidean metrics and identification ℝ^n×ℝ=ℝ^(n+1), dimH(E×[0,1])=dimH(E)+1; equivalently dimH(appendCoord(n) '' (E×I))=dimH(E)+1. Both dimensions are finite, so this is also the equality of their real values.

hypotheses.statement: E is compact in the Euclidean space Ambient n=ℝ^n.

definitions.type: ℕ → real finite dimensional inner product spaces
definitions.definition: Ambient(m)=EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m), the space of m real coordinates with norm ‖x‖₂=(Σ_{j<m}|x_j|²)^(1/2). The sum is zero when m=0. Distances are norms of differences. More generally the native EuclideanSpace k (Fin m), for a real-or-complex-like field k, is the m-coordinate k-space with this same sum-of-squared-absolute-values norm; its scalar vector-space structure is coordinatewise.

binders.type: vector in the indicated real or k-valued coordinate space

definitions.type: extended diameter of a subset of any pseudo extended metric space
definitions.definition: For a pseudo extended metric space Z and B⊆Z, ediam(B)=sup{edist(x,y):x∈B,y∈B} in [0,∞], with supremum of the empty set zero. For finite ediam, diam(B)=(ediam B).toReal and ediam B=ofReal(diam B). In metric spaces edist is ofReal of the ordinary distance.
ofReal(v) is max(v,0) embedded in the extended nonnegative reals. The notation z.toReal for z∈[0,∞] is its real value when finite, and zero for z=∞.

definitions.type: real exponent × extended scale × subset of an extended metric space → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: For an extended metric space Z, exponent u∈ℝ, scale h∈[0,∞], and B⊆Z, Content(u,h,B)=inf_{U:ℕ→Set Z; B⊆⋃_i U_i; ∀i ediam(U_i)≤h} Σ_i sup_{(_ : U_i nonempty)} (ediam U_i)^u. Infima, suprema and sums are in [0,∞]; an infimum over no covers is ∞. This is exactly the Content in basis-registry.json /lean_header. Countable covers may be padded by empty sets.

definitions.type: real exponent × real scale × subset → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: C_u(h,B), also written C_u(h,B), means Content(u,ofReal h,B) for real scale h. We use it only at h>0.

binders.type: subset of an extended metric space

definitions.type: real exponent × subset of a Borel extended metric space → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: H^u(B)=μH[u](B) denotes Mathlib's unnormalized Hausdorff measure, the metric measure mkMetric for the gauge r↦r^u on the Borel sigma algebra. The metric-measure construction takes countable-cover outer contents for this gauge, with the empty-set gauge cost forced to zero, and their supremum as the scale tends to zero. Its precise cover evaluation will be applied as an explicit native source, rather than assumed as an extra premise. No spherical or dimensional normalization factor is used.

binders.type: subset of a Borel extended metric space

definitions.type: subset of an extended metric space → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: For B in an extended metric space, equipped with its Borel measurable structure when computing H, dimH(B)=sup{d∈[0,∞): H^d(B)=∞}, the supremum taken in [0,∞] and with sup ∅=0. This is native Mathlib dimH. Positive-exponent critical-exponent directions are invoked as explicit native sources. We use no zero-exponent measure assertion.

binders.type: subset of an extended metric space

definitions.type: subset of ℝ
definitions.definition: I=[0,1]={t∈ℝ:0≤t≤1}. This is unitInterval in the basis header.

definitions.type: metric space → metric spaces
definitions.definition: For a metric space Z, MaxProd(Z)=Z×ℝ with distance d_max((x,t),(y,u))=max(d_Z(x,y),|t−u|). For B⊆Z, B×I always denotes a subset of MaxProd(Z) in intermediate lemmas. All metric spaces in integration or Hausdorff-measure statements carry their Borel sigma algebra.

definitions.type: for m∈ℕ, MaxProd(Ambient m) → Ambient(m+1)
definitions.definition: appendCoord(m)(x,t) is the vector whose first m coordinates are those of x and whose last coordinate is t. In the exact basis header it is WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.lastCases t (fun j => x j)). Its target always carries the Euclidean norm; its source here carries the maximum metric. It is a total coordinate construction, including m=0. Under the problem's identification ℝ^n×ℝ=ℝ^(n+1), the Euclidean set E×[0,1] is appendCoord(n) '' (E×I).

definitions.type: measure on the Borel sets of ℝ
definitions.definition: volume is Lebesgue measure on ℝ, with its usual Borel measurable structure (and its extension as an outer measure on arbitrary sets). Thus measure monotonicity applies to all subsets; no measurability of a covering set is implicit.

definitions.type: subset × constant → functions
definitions.definition: For a set B⊆Z and a scalar c∈[0,∞], c1_B denotes the function equal to c on B and zero off B, that is B.indicator(fun _ => c). This is meaningful for c=∞ as well, with no subtraction of infinities.

definitions.type: measure × nonnegative extended function → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: For a measurable space Z, measure μ and f:Z→[0,∞], ∫⁻ f dμ (the lower Lebesgue integral, lintegral) is the supremum of ∫g dμ over measurable nonnegative simple functions g≤f; a simple function integral is its finite sum of values times the measures of the corresponding disjoint level sets. All integrals in the slicing proof are lower integrals; integrability is never required.

binders.type: nonnegative measurable simple function on Z

definitions.type: nonnegative real × map of pseudo extended metric spaces → propositions
definitions.definition: LipschitzWith(K,f) means ∀x,y, edist(f x,f y)≤K·edist(x,y), where K is a finite nonnegative real embedded into [0,∞]. On metric spaces this is the usual distance inequality.

binders.type: map between pseudo extended metric spaces

definitions.type: nonnegative real × map of extended metric spaces → propositions
definitions.definition: AntilipschitzWith(L,f) means ∀x,y, edist(x,y)≤L·edist(f x,f y), with finite L≥0. On metric spaces this is the corresponding ordinary distance inequality.

definitions.type: ordered field or real vector space × endpoints → subsets
definitions.definition: segment(k,x,y)={a•x+b•y: a,b∈k, a≥0,b≥0,a+b=1}, in a vector space over an ordered scalar field k; over ℝ this is the usual closed line segment.

definitions.type: field × vector space → ℕ
definitions.definition: finrank(k,Z) is the dimension as a natural number of a finite-dimensional k-vector space Z (and is zero by the native total convention if the vector-space rank is infinite). In this proof its arguments are finite dimensional.

definitions.type: real or extended nonnegative base × real exponent → corresponding scalars
definitions.definition: The notation v^u uses the standard real power; on positive real v it is exp(u log v), with 0^u=0 for u>0 and 0^0=1. For extended nonnegative bases it is the usual extension: at u>0, ∞^u=∞ and 0^u=0; at u=0 the value is 1; at u<0, 0^u=∞ and ∞^u=0. Only nonnegative real bases and positive exponents occur in the covering calculations. The native real function at negative v is defined using |v|, as in Real.rpow.

R004.fact: For every natural n, the real coordinate space Ambient n with its given Euclidean inner product and norm is a finite-dimensional real normed vector space. Its coordinate vectors e_j, j∈Fin n, form a basis, including the empty basis for n=0; its metric also supplies an extended metric.

grounds.reason: n is a natural number, including zero, so Fin n is finite.
Ambient n is the real coordinate space with coordinatewise vector operations and its Euclidean inner product/norm.

R004.justification: Define e_j to have coordinate 1 at j and 0 elsewhere. Each x equals the finite sum Σ_j x_j e_j by evaluation at each coordinate. If Σ_j a_j e_j=0, evaluation at j gives a_j=0, proving independence. For n=0 every vector is the unique empty tuple, and spanning and independence hold for the empty family. Hence the space is finite dimensional. The supplied Euclidean inner product induces the displayed norm and the compatible real normed-space structure. Regard each finite real distance as an extended nonnegative distance to obtain the extended metric, preserving the metric axioms.

R005.fact: The real numbers with norm |x| and their usual addition and real scalar multiplication form a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, of dimension one, with basis consisting of 1.

grounds.reason: S001 explicitly takes the ambient space to be ℝ, with the standard real normed-space interpretation.
The supplied M012 statement requires the ambient real normed space to be finite dimensional; the present routine verification supplies precisely this condition for ℝ.

R005.justification: The real field operations give the real vector-space and additive-group laws. Absolute value is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at zero, is subadditive, and satisfies |a x|=|a||x|, so it gives the stated compatible norm. Every real x equals x·1, and a·1=0 implies a=0. Thus the singleton 1 spans and is linearly independent, proving finite dimensionality.

R101.fact: For the D004 infimum, enlarging the allowed scale decreases Content. Its supremum over positive extended scales equals its supremum over scales ofReal δ with real δ>0.

grounds.reason: Admissibility is the diameter upper bound; the value is an infimum in [0,∞].
The proof gives a positive finite δ with ofReal δ≤h for every positive extended h.

R101.justification: Every cover allowed at a smaller scale is allowed at a larger scale, so the larger-scale infimum is no greater. Each positive real scale occurs among the extended scales. Conversely each extended-scale content is bounded above by the content at the displayed smaller positive real scale. Taking suprema gives both inequalities.

R101.fact: If an infimum of admissible cover costs in [0,∞] equals zero, then for every real t>0 an admissible cover has cost <ofReal t.

grounds.reason: F001 expresses H as a supremum of nonnegative real-scale contents.
L2 gives H=0 and r,ε>0; hence the content at r/2 is zero and t=ε/4 is positive.

R101.justification: Each content is bounded above by the zero supremum and below by zero. If no admissible cost were below ofReal t, that positive number would be a lower bound for all costs, contradicting infimum zero. The empty family has infimum ∞, so cannot be the family here.

R101.fact: If z≤ofReal(r/2) with real r>0, then z is finite, d=z.toReal satisfies 0≤d≤r/2 and z=ofReal d. For s>0, (ofReal d)^s=ofReal(d^s).

grounds.reason: D002 supplies finite-diameter conversion.
D003 defines the finite embedding and toReal.
D018 specifies the corresponding real and extended powers.
F002 bounds every diameter by ofReal(r/2).

R101.justification: The upper bound is finite, so toReal is the inverse order-preserving real coordinate and gives the stated bounds. At d=0 both powers are zero since s>0. At d>0 both use the same positive real power, and the embedding preserves its value. This verifies the termwise cost conversion.

R101.fact: For ε>0 and e_i=ε·2^(−i−3), each e_i>0 and the real and extended nonnegative sums equal ε/4 and ofReal(ε/4), respectively.

grounds.reason: L2 gives ε>0.
S003 defines e and displays its finite partial sum (ε/4)(1−2^(−m)).

R101.justification: The displayed finite geometric identity follows by multiplying the partial sum by 1−1/2. The sequence 2^(−m) tends to zero (for example 2^m≥m+1 gives the elementary reciprocal bound). Thus the nonnegative partial sums increase to ε/4. Their supremum is the extended nonnegative sum, yielding the same finite embedded value.

R101.fact: For every i, continuity of x↦x^s at d_i, e_i>0 and d_i<r yield a_i with d_i<a_i<r and a_i^s<d_i^s+e_i; these choices may be made as a sequence.

grounds.reason: M020 supplies continuity once s≥0.
L1 gives s>0.
F003 supplies the real d_i, e_i>0, and d_i<r.

R101.justification: Continuity gives a radius ρ_i>0 for error e_i. Take η_i=(1/2)min(ρ_i,r−d_i)>0. Then η_i<ρ_i and η_i<r−d_i, so a_i=d_i+η_i has the claimed interval and power bounds. Ordinary countable choice of the established nonempty radius choices produces the sequence, as explicitly used in S004; no uniform radius or enlarged covering set is needed.

R101.fact: For nonnegative real sequences b_i,c_i,f_i with f_i≤b_i+c_i and finite totals B=Σ_i ofReal b_i, C=Σ_i ofReal c_i, one has Σ_i ofReal f_i≤B+C. In this application B<ofReal(ε/4), C=ofReal(ε/4), hence the budget total is <ofReal ε.

grounds.reason: F003 gives nonnegative d_i, positive errors, the bound on the original total and the finite error total.
F004 gives positive a_i and a_i^s<d_i^s+e_i.
s>0 ensures all these real powers are nonnegative.

R101.justification: For every finite initial segment, monotonicity and finite addition give the corresponding sum bound. Nonnegative series are suprema of these partial sums. The partial sums of b and c increase to their finite totals, so their sums increase to B+C; taking suprema proves the claimed weak bound. With b_i=d_i^s, c_i=e_i and f_i=a_i^s, finite scalar addition and ε>0 give B+C<ofReal(ε/2)<ofReal ε. No interchange involving signed terms or infinite strict addition is used.

R102.fact: If d is an extended nonnegative real, delta is a finite nonnegative real and d<=ofReal(delta), then d is finite, 0<=d.toReal<=delta and ofReal(d.toReal)=d. For finite nonnegative reals a,b, ofReal(a)<=ofReal(b) is equivalent to a<=b.

grounds.reason: L1 gives delta>0 and L2 bounds each d=ediam(V_i) by ofReal(delta).
D003 identifies finite extended nonnegative values with their real values.

R102.justification: The finite bound excludes the top element. The order-preserving identification of the finite nonnegative part with the nonnegative real half-line gives the two inequalities and inverse conversion. This also permits passing from a pointwise edist bound to the real absolute-distance bound used in S002.

R102.fact: The real numbers with their usual order and metric bornology form an order bornology: metric-bounded sets are order-bounded, and every interval with finite real endpoints is metric-bounded. Thus the real structure satisfies the structural order/bornology premise of M018.

grounds.reason: M018 requires a conditionally complete lattice with compatible bornology.
Each Bproj_i is contained in a finite interval in its nonempty branch.

R102.justification: A real set lying in a ball of radius R about a lies in [a-R,a+R]. Conversely a set contained between real bounds p,q has distances from p bounded by max(q-p,0). The usual real order is conditionally complete. These facts identify the order and metric boundedness structures used in the stated application.

R102.fact: For arbitrary finite real endpoints a,b the interval [a,b] is closed, hence Borel measurable, also when empty. The empty set and finite intersections of such sets are Borel measurable.

grounds.reason: J_i is either empty or a closed real interval; I=[0,1].
D008 defines I.
D011 fixes the Borel measurable structure on R.

R102.justification: The complement of [a,b] is the union of the open rays (-infinity,a) and (b,infinity). Closed sets are complements of open sets and belong to the Borel sigma algebra, which is closed under finite intersections.

R102.fact: For u>0, the map d -> d^u is increasing on extended nonnegative reals. For finite r>=0, (ofReal(r))^u=ofReal(r^u); also (ofReal(r^u))*ofReal(r)=ofReal(r^(u+1)).

grounds.reason: F001 gives finite 0<=rho_i<=delta and the projection diameter bounds.
L1 gives s>0, hence s+1>0.
D018 supplies the standard power conventions.

R102.justification: On positive finite bases, monotonicity follows from increasing log and exp and multiplication by u>0. The identity r^u*r=r^(u+1) follows by adding exponents in exp(u log r). At r=0 both positive powers vanish, and the extended endpoints follow from 0^u=0 and infinity^u=infinity. Embedding finite nonnegative reals preserves products and the defined powers. These facts justify both the slice-cost comparison here and the termwise power identity in S005.

R102.fact: For any measurable set B in a measurable space and fixed k in [0,infinity], the function k1_B with values in [0,infinity] is measurable, including k=infinity. A measurable function is almost-everywhere measurable for every measure.

grounds.reason: F003 supplies measurability of I and every J_i intersect I.
h and g_i are exactly constant indicators on those sets.
D012 defines an indicator by its values, including an infinite constant.

R102.justification: The inverse image of a Borel set under k1_B is one of the empty set, B, its complement, or the entire space, depending on membership of 0 and k. All are measurable. Almost-everywhere measurability then holds using the function itself as the measurable representative, with no exceptional set.

R102.fact: Multiplication by a fixed nonnegative extended scalar preserves inequalities (with 0*infinity=0). For sequences a_i<=b_i in [0,infinity], sum_i a_i<=sum_i b_i, without finiteness assumptions.

grounds.reason: F003 bounds volume(J_i) by ofReal(rho_i).
The displayed chain multiplies measure inequalities by nonnegative ofReal(rho_i^s) and then sums.
D011 supplies measure monotonicity on J_i intersect I subset J_i.

R102.justification: For finite nonnegative scalars multiplication is order preserving; the zero and infinity cases satisfy the same inequality directly under the stated conventions. Compare each finite partial sum termwise, then take the supremum over finite index sets, which defines the nonnegative extended sum.

R102.fact: In [0,infinity], if c<=k for every member k of a family K, then c<=inf K, including K empty with inf K=infinity. If f(delta)<=g(delta) for every delta>0, then sup_{delta>0} f(delta)<=sup_{delta>0} g(delta), including infinite suprema.

grounds.reason: F005 makes C_s(delta,A) a lower bound for every admissible product-cover cost.
N101 identifies these infima with the positive-exponent contents and identifies the scale suprema with H.
The scale inequality has been proved for arbitrary positive delta and s+1 is positive.

R102.justification: An infimum is the greatest lower bound, so every lower bound is below it; for an empty family this says only c<=infinity. Each f(delta) is below the supremum of g, making that supremum an upper bound for all f(delta); the least-upper-bound property yields the stated supremum inequality. No interchange of infimum, supremum or integral is involved.

R103.fact: For 0<a≤1, the natural ceiling N=ceil(1/a) is finite and satisfies N≥1, 1/N≤a and N≤1/a+1≤2/a. The N closed intervals [j/N,(j+1)/N], 0≤j<N, cover [0,1] and have diameter 1/N.

grounds.reason: F001 supplies 0<a_i≤r for the chosen budgets.
r=min(1,δ), with δ>0, gives r≤1.

R103.justification: The Archimedean property of the reals gives the least natural integer N≥1/a; its minimality gives N<1/a+1. Positivity permits reciprocation to obtain 1/N≤a. Adjacent interval endpoints agree, their first endpoint is zero and last is one, so their finite union is [0,1]. Distances in each interval are at most its endpoint difference, attained by its endpoints.

R103.fact: If ediam U≤ofReal a with finite a≥0 and J is a real interval of length b≤a, then ediam(U×J)≤ofReal a in MaxProd X. This also holds when U is empty.

grounds.reason: The selected pair supplies ediam U_i≤ofReal a_i and a_i>0.
The constructed intervals have length 1/N_i≤a_i.
Extended diameter is the supremum of pairwise extended distances.
The product distance is the maximum of the two component distances.

R103.justification: Every pair from U has distance ≤a by the diameter bound and the order-preserving embedding of nonnegative finite reals. Every pair from J has distance ≤b≤a. Hence each product distance, their maximum, is ≤a, and taking its supremum preserves the upper bound. An empty product has diameter zero.

R103.fact: For p>0 the extended nonnegative power x↦x^p is increasing. For finite a>0, (ofReal a)^p=ofReal(a^p), and for q>0 one has a^(q+1)=a*a^q. Consequently, N finite product sets each of diameter ≤ofReal a have total p-cost ≤ofReal(N*a^p), including empty sets when p>0.

grounds.reason: L1 gives q>0; thus p=q+1>0.
The chosen budgets are strictly positive finite reals.
The product diameter bounds and finite positive integers N_i have been established.
Real powers use exp(p log a) on positive bases and zero at base zero for positive exponents.

R103.justification: Monotonicity of log and exp proves power monotonicity for positive finite bases; the specified zero and infinity values give the endpoints. The exponential addition law gives a^(q+1)=a*a^q. Embedding nonnegative finite values commutes with these powers and finite sums. Bounding each of N costs and summing gives the stated inequality; empty-set cost is zero.

R103.fact: For finite natural N_i≥1, the set T={(i,j):i∈ℕ,j<N_i} has a natural enumeration without repetitions. For nonnegative extended costs c_(i,j), enumeration preserves the total sum and Σ_T c=Σ_i Σ_(j<N_i)c_(i,j). Nonnegative sums preserve termwise inequalities and commute with multiplication by a finite positive constant, in particular 2.

grounds.reason: Each N_i is a finite positive natural; all product costs and comparison terms lie in [0,∞].
Cover costs are nonnegative extended sums over natural indices.

R103.justification: List pairs in successive finite diagonals of ℕ×ℕ and retain exactly those in T. Every admissible pair occurs once; the pairs (i,0) show that the retained list is infinite. A nonnegative sum is the supremum of its finite subsums, so a bijection preserves it. Every finite set of pairs is contained in finitely many complete finite rows; conversely such rows form a finite set of pairs. This gives the regrouping identity. Termwise comparison follows on finite subsums. Multiplication by a fixed positive finite constant is an order isomorphism of [0,∞], hence preserves their suprema and gives the scaling identity.

R103.fact: If z∈[0,∞] satisfies z≤ofReal(2ε) for every real ε>0, then z=0.

grounds.reason: F002 supplies a cover of cost <ofReal(2ε) for every positive ε at the fixed positive scale.
N101 identifies the relevant content with the infimum of these cover costs.

R103.justification: Choosing ε=1 bounds z by the finite value 2, excluding infinity. If its finite real value t were positive, ε=t/4 would give t≤t/2, a contradiction. Nonnegativity therefore forces z=0. The subsequent supremum is a supremum of zero contents by N101, without any exchange of limits or integrals.

R104.fact: For a metric space X, d((x,t),(y,u))=max(d_X(x,y),|t−u|) is a finite metric on X×ℝ. The usual real metric and this product metric induce extended metrics, so the supplied extended-metric dimension statements apply to them.

grounds.reason: X is an arbitrary metric space.
D009 specifies exactly this product set and distance; the real factor has its usual metric.

R104.justification: Nonnegativity and symmetry follow from those of each factor. The maximum vanishes exactly when both factor distances vanish, hence exactly when both coordinates coincide. For three points the two factor triangle inequalities and max(a+c,b+d)≤max(a,b)+max(c,d) prove the product triangle inequality. All distances are finite. Embedding a finite nonnegative distance into [0,∞] preserves zero, order and addition, yielding the corresponding extended metric axioms.

R105.fact: For z∈[0,∞] with z≠∞, z.toReal≥0 and ofReal(z.toReal)=z. For nonnegative real a,b, ofReal a≤ofReal b iff a≤b, likewise for strict inequality, and ofReal(a+b)=ofReal a+ofReal b. Every ofReal b is finite; consequently z≤ofReal b implies z≠∞. Also 0≠∞ and ∞≤z implies z=∞.

grounds.reason: D003 defines ofReal as the nonnegative real embedding and toReal as the finite real value, with infinity the added top element.
D007 places dimH in [0,∞].
L1 provides dimH A≠∞, the actual condition for recovering dimH A from D0.

R105.justification: The extended nonnegative reals consist of the nonnegative reals and an added largest element infinity. On finite nonnegative values, the embedding and finite-value map are inverse and the order and addition are the real ones. A finite embedded value is strictly below infinity, so a value bounded by it cannot be infinity. Top-element antisymmetry gives the last implication. These facts justify the initial identification and subsequent finite-value comparisons and addition; S004 establishes product finiteness before applying the finite inverse there.

R105.fact: For any metric space X, the formula d((x,t),(y,u))=max(d_X(x,y),|t−u|) makes X×ℝ a metric space and hence an extended metric space via edist=ofReal d. Equipping it with its own Borel sigma algebra satisfies the Borel-space premises of M004 and M005 without any assumption on the subset G.

grounds.reason: X is an arbitrary metric space with its Borel sigma algebra.
D009 specifies this maximum distance and chooses the Borel sigma algebra for Hausdorff-measure statements.
D002 identifies metric edist with ofReal of distance.

R105.justification: Nonnegativity and symmetry hold in each coordinate; distance zero forces both coordinates equal. Each coordinate distance obeys the triangle inequality and is bounded by the maximum on its corresponding leg, so both coordinate distances across a triangle are bounded by the sum of the two leg maxima; taking their maximum proves the product triangle inequality. Embedding the nonnegative metric distances gives the extended metric inequalities. The sigma algebra generated by this metric's open sets is its Borel structure by construction; no product-sigma-algebra identification or measurability of G is needed.

R106.fact: For a,b,d≥0 with d²=a²+b² and m=max(a,b), one has m≤d≤√2·m. Here √2 is finite nonnegative and (√2)²=2.

grounds.reason: a and b are respectively a Euclidean norm and an absolute value; d is the Euclidean target distance, and the displayed finite-sum computation establishes d²=a²+b².
The norm is the nonnegative square root of the finite sum of coordinate squares.

R106.justification: Since 0≤a,b≤m and m is one of a,b, m²≤a²+b²≤2m²=(√2·m)². Squaring preserves and reflects order between nonnegative reals: if 0≤x<y then y²−x²=(y−x)(y+x)>0. Apply this to the two inequalities. These are exactly the square-root and sign conditions used in S001.

R106.fact: If (Z,d) is a metric space, then d_max((x,t),(y,u))=max(d(x,y),|t−u|) is a metric on Z×ℝ; its finite distances canonically define an extended metric. Thus MaxProd(Ambient n) and Ambient(n+1) satisfy the space hypotheses of M006/M007 for every n≥0.

grounds.reason: Ambient m is the specified Euclidean inner product space with its norm distance, for all natural m including zero.
MaxProd uses exactly the maximum of the given metric distance and real absolute difference.

R106.justification: Nonnegativity and symmetry follow for each component. A zero maximum forces both component distances to vanish, hence equality of both coordinates. Each component distance across three points is at most the sum of the corresponding two component distances, which is at most the sum of the two maxima; taking the maximum proves the triangle inequality. Embedding nonnegative finite distances into [0,∞] preserves these metric axioms. No dimension or nonemptiness condition is introduced.

R107.fact: For finite a,b∈[0,∞], if b=a+1 then b.toReal=a.toReal+1, and a+1 is finite. Here a=dimH(E) and b=dimH(appendCoord(n) '' (E×I)).

grounds.reason: D003 identifies finite extended nonnegative reals with their real values.
N004 supplies finiteness of dimH(E).
N105 supplies finiteness and the dimension equality for the maximum product.
N106 transfers that product dimension, hence its finiteness and equality, to the Euclidean image.

R107.justification: Finite extended nonnegative reals are nonnegative real numbers under the canonical embedding. Their finite sums agree with real addition; the sum of the finite representatives a.toReal and 1 is finite. Applying the inverse real-value identification to b=a+1 gives the stated equality.

1: # Hausdorff dimension of a product with an interval
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Elias M. Stein and Rami Shakarchi, *Real Analysis: Measure Theory,
6: Integration, and Hilbert Spaces*, Princeton Lectures in Analysis III,
7: Chapter 7, Problems, exercise 9, printed page 388.
8: Book DOI: [10.1515/9781400835560](https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400835560).
9: 
10: > 9. Let \(E\) be a compact set in \(\mathbb R^{d-1}\). Show that
11: > \(\dim(E\times I)=\dim(E)+1\), where \(I\) is the unit interval in
12: > \(\mathbb R\).
13: 
14: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
15: 
16: Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
17: 2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
18: \(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
19: the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.
20: 
21: Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
22: compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
23: with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove
24: 
25: \[
26: \dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
27: \]
28: 
29: The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
30: formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
31: 
32: ## Fixed natural-language proof
33: 
34: For a Euclidean set \(A\), exponent \(s>0\), and scale \(\delta>0\), put
35: 
36: \[
37: H^s_\delta(A)=\inf\left\{\sum_i(\operatorname{diam}U_i)^s:
38:  A\subseteq\bigcup_iU_i,\quad\operatorname{diam}U_i\leq\delta\right\},
39: \qquad H^s(A)=\sup_{\delta>0}H^s_\delta(A).
40: \]
41: 
42: Covers are countable, with empty members contributing zero. This
43: unnormalized Hausdorff measure gives the usual Hausdorff dimension. We use
44: its critical-exponent characterization: \(H^s(A)=0\) if
45: \(s>\dim_H A\), and \(H^s(A)=\infty\) if \(0<s<\dim_H A\).
46: Conversely, zero measure implies \(\dim_H A\leq s\), and infinite
47: measure implies \(\dim_H A\geq s\).
48: 
49: Write \(D=\dim_H E\) and \(F=E\times[0,1]\). First \(0\leq D\leq n\).
50: Indeed, compactness makes \(E\) bounded. When \(n>0\), a box containing
51: it admits a cover by at most \(Ch^{-n}\) cubes of side at most \(h\),
52: for \(0<h\leq1\). Here \(C\) depends only on that box. Each cube has
53: diameter at most \(\sqrt n h\). For any \(s>n\), the total \(s\)-cost
54: is at most \(C n^{s/2}h^{s-n}\to0\). These arbitrarily fine covers
55: give \(H^s(E)=0\) and hence \(D\leq n\). If \(n=0\), nonemptiness
56: makes \(E=\mathbb R^0\), a singleton of zero \(s\)-cost for every
57: \(s>0\); thus \(D=0\).
58: 
59: ### Upper bound
60: 
61: When \(n=0\), \(F\) is isometric to \([0,1]\). Dividing this interval
62: into \(N\) equal pieces gives total \(a\)-cost \(N^{1-a}\to0\) for
63: every \(a>1\), proving \(\dim_H F\leq1=D+1\).
64: For this upper-bound argument now assume \(n\geq1\).
65: 
66: Fix \(q>D\). Since \(q>0\) and \(H^q(E)=0\), for every
67: \(0<r\leq1\) and \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a countable cover
68: \((U_i)\) of \(E\) with nonempty-member diameters
69: \(0<r_i\leq r\) and \(\sum_i r_i^q<\varepsilon\).
70: The positive-diameter requirement costs nothing: start with a cover of
71: cost below \(\varepsilon/2\); replace each zero-diameter singleton by
72: a ball of diameter at most \(r\), choosing the \(i\)-th replacement
73: to have \(q\)-cost less than \(\varepsilon2^{-i-2}\). The added cost
74: is less than \(\varepsilon/2\). Discard empty members.
75: 
76: Let \(N_i=\lceil1/r_i\rceil\). Partition \([0,1]\) into \(N_i\)
77: closed intervals of length \(1/N_i\leq r_i\). Because \(r_i\leq1\),
78: \(N_i\leq2/r_i\). The corresponding products with \(U_i\) form a
79: countable cover of \(F\). Each has Euclidean diameter at most
80: \(\sqrt2 r_i\), and their total \((q+1)\)-cost is at most
81: 
82: \[
83: \sum_iN_i(\sqrt2 r_i)^{q+1}
84: \leq2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\sum_i r_i^q
85: <2(\sqrt2)^{q+1}\varepsilon.
86: \]
87: 
88: For any target scale \(\delta>0\), choose
89: \(r\leq\min(1,\delta/\sqrt2)\), then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
90: Thus \(H^{q+1}_\delta(F)=0\) for every scale, so
91: \(H^{q+1}(F)=0\) and \(\dim_H F\leq q+1\). Letting \(q\downarrow D\)
92: gives \(\dim_H F\leq D+1\).
93: 
94: ### Lower bound when \(D>0\)
95: 
96: Fix \(0<s<D\). Then \(H^s(E)=\infty\), so
97: \(H^s_\delta(E)\) becomes arbitrarily large as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
98: We claim that, for every \(\delta>0\),
99: 
100: \[
101: H^s_\delta(E)\leq H^{s+1}_\delta(F).                 \tag{1}
102: \]
103: 
104: Take an arbitrary countable \(\delta\)-cover \((V_i)_{i\geq0}\) of
105: \(F\), discarding empty members. Define
106: \(\rho_i=\operatorname{diam}V_i\),
107: \(A_i=\pi_{\mathbb R^n}(V_i)\), and
108: \(B_i=\pi_{\mathbb R}(V_i)\). Coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz,
109: so both projected diameters are at most \(\rho_i\leq\delta\).
110: For \(\varepsilon>0\), put
111: 
112: \[
113: \eta_i=\frac{\varepsilon2^{-i-1}}{1+\rho_i^s}>0.
114: \]
115: 
116: Enclose \(B_i\) in an open interval \(J_i\) of length at most
117: \(\rho_i+\eta_i\): its supremum minus infimum is at most \(\rho_i\),
118: and an enlargement of total width \(\eta_i\) suffices. This avoids
119: assuming that the arbitrary covering sets or their projections are measurable.
120: 
121: For each \(t\in[0,1]\), the sets \(A_i\) for which \(t\in J_i\)
122: cover \(E\). Indeed, a point \((x,t)\in F\) belongs to some \(V_i\),
123: giving \(x\in A_i\) and \(t\in B_i\subset J_i\). Their diameters
124: are at most \(\rho_i\). Consequently, with \(c=H^s_\delta(E)\),
125: 
126: \[
127: c\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s\mathbf1_{J_i}(t)\quad(t\in[0,1]).
128: \]
129: 
130: The constant \(c\) is finite: compactness gives a finite cover of \(E\)
131: by balls of diameter at most \(\delta\), with finite \(s\)-cost.
132: Each summand is nonnegative and measurable since \(J_i\) is open.
133: Integrate over \([0,1]\), of Lebesgue measure one, and use Tonelli's
134: theorem for this nonnegative series. Since
135: \(|J_i\cap[0,1]|\leq\rho_i+\eta_i\),
136: 
137: \[
138: \begin{aligned}
139: c&\leq\sum_i\rho_i^s|J_i\cap[0,1]|\\
140:  &\leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\sum_i\eta_i\rho_i^s
141:  \leq\sum_i\rho_i^{s+1}+\varepsilon.
142: \end{aligned}
143: \]
144: 
145: If the first series is infinite the desired inequality is immediate;
146: otherwise let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\). Take the infimum over the
147: arbitrary covers to obtain (1). As its left side is unbounded at small
148: scales, \(H^{s+1}(F)=\infty\), giving \(\dim_H F\geq s+1\).
149: Letting \(s\uparrow D\) proves \(\dim_H F\geq D+1\).
150: 
151: ### Lower bound when \(D=0\)
152: 
153: Choose \(x_0\in E\). The map \(t\mapsto(x_0,t)\) is an isometric
154: embedding of \([0,1]\) into \(F\), so dimension monotonicity gives
155: \(\dim_H F\geq\dim_H[0,1]\). This interval has dimension one:
156: equal-length covers gave the upper bound above. For \(0<s<1\), any
157: \(\delta\)-cover with diameters \(\rho_i\leq\delta\) satisfies
158: \(\sum_i\rho_i\geq1\). To see this, enclose its nonempty members
159: in open intervals of lengths at most \(\rho_i+\varepsilon2^{-i-1}\),
160: use countable subadditivity of length to get
161: \(1\leq\sum_i\rho_i+\varepsilon\), and let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\).
162: Hence \(\sum_i\rho_i^s\geq\delta^{s-1}\sum_i\rho_i
163: \geq\delta^{s-1}\to\infty\) as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
164: This proves the lower bound one. Thus \(\dim_H F\geq1=D+1\),
165: including when \(n=0\).
166: 
167: Together the bounds establish the required equality.
168: 
169: ## Input status
170: 
171: This file fixes the problem, conventions and supplied proof route for future
172: tests. It is a natural-language input, not an NL0 artifact, an Audit A receipt,
173: a Lean proof, or a passing test result. Future runs must independently produce
174: and check those artifacts. The basic Hausdorff-measure and integration facts
175: used here must be registered by that future NL0/Audit A workflow.

1: We prove the exact full_target with its original assumptions: n is any natural number (zero is allowed), E⊆ℝ^n is nonempty and compact, and I=[0,1]. We model Euclidean ℝ^n by Ambient n=EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n). The final ambient metric is Euclidean. In the intermediate argument only, X×ℝ carries the maximum product metric d((x,t),(y,u))=max(d_X(x,y),|t−u|). Section 6 proves the required change of metric, with explicit constants. Compactness remains an original hypothesis; the new argument happens to prove the result for all nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space and so does not need compactness.
2: 
3: Definitions and normalization. All measure values and countable sums of nonnegative costs may lie in [0,∞]. For s>0 define C_s(δ,A)=Content(s,ofReal δ,A), for real δ>0, using the countable-cover infimum in lean_header. Define H^s(A)=μH[s](A), Mathlib's unnormalized Hausdorff measure. For positive s the guard sup_{U_i nonempty} (ediam U_i)^s in that formula is exactly (ediam U_i)^s: the only difference could occur for an empty U_i, whose diameter and positive power are both zero. Thus the definitions agree with the unnormalized countable-cover definitions in problem.md, not a normalized spherical measure. We never need the exponent-zero measure. Hausdorff dimension is Mathlib dimH with values in [0,∞]; by B002 this has the stipulated critical-exponent meaning. The final dimensions are finite by B004 and the proved upper bound. Accordingly their equality in [0,∞] is the original real-valued equality as well.
4: 
5: §1. Derivation of B101 (cover content and positive budgets).
6: For each s>0 the preceding guard observation identifies C_s with the raw cover infimum. If 0<δ₁≤δ₂, every δ₁-cover is also a δ₂-cover, hence C_s(δ₂,A)≤C_s(δ₁,A). B001 says H^s is the supremum over all positive extended scales. The same supremum is obtained from finite positive real scales: those are included in all extended scales, and every positive extended scale r admits a finite positive real δ with ofReal δ≤r, so its content is bounded by the content at δ. These observations prove both the identification and the stated supremum formula.
7: 
8: Now let q>0, H^q(A)=0, r>0 and ε>0. The content at r/2 is zero. By the defining property of the infimum there is a countable cover U_i with ediam U_i≤ofReal(r/2) and total q-cost <ofReal(ε/4). In particular all diameters are finite. Write d_i=(ediam U_i).toReal, so 0≤d_i≤r/2 and ediam U_i=ofReal d_i. For each i put e_i=ε·2^(−i−3), with i starting at zero, so e_i>0 and Σ_i e_i=ε/4. By B010, continuity of x↦x^q at d_i and the strict gap d_i<r allow a choice a_i with d_i<a_i≤r and a_i^q<d_i^q+e_i. To be explicit, take η_i>0 sufficiently small that η_i<r−d_i and |(d_i+η_i)^q−d_i^q|<e_i, and put a_i=d_i+η_i. Such choices are independent for each natural index. Empty covering members are harmless and receive their own positive numerical budgets. Summing nonnegative inequalities gives Σ_i ofReal(a_i^q)≤Σ_i ofReal(d_i^q)+ofReal(ε/4)<ofReal(ε/2)<ofReal ε. The geometric series identity follows by summing its first m terms, (ε/4)(1−2^(−m)), and letting m tend to infinity. No positive diameter of an actual set is required. This proves B101, including for a zero-dimensional or singleton space.
9: 
10: §2. Derivation of B102 (slicing inequality).
11: Fix any metric space X, subset A, s>0 and finite δ>0. Let V_i be any countable δ-cover of A×I in the maximum product metric. Empty V_i will contribute zero throughout; all hulls and weights mentioned below are assigned the empty set and zero for such indices. For a nonempty V_i write ρ_i=(ediam V_i).toReal∈[0,δ], A_i=π_X(V_i), and B_i=π_ℝ(V_i). Coordinate projections are 1-Lipschitz, because each coordinate distance is bounded by the maximum distance. B011 therefore gives ediam A_i≤ofReal ρ_i and ediam B_i≤ofReal ρ_i.
12: 
13: The nonempty real set B_i is bounded: choose t_i∈B_i, and then every t∈B_i satisfies |t−t_i|≤ρ_i; this uses the definition of diameter and its finiteness. Let J_i=[inf B_i,sup B_i]. B009 gives B_i⊆J_i and volume(J_i)=ediam B_i≤ofReal ρ_i. Each J_i is closed and measurable, although B_i and V_i need not be measurable. Empty V_i have J_i=∅ as stipulated.
14: 
15: Fix t∈I. The sets A_i with t∈J_i cover A: for each x∈A, choose a cover member containing (x,t); it is nonempty and gives x∈A_i and t∈B_i⊆J_i. Represent this subfamily as the natural-indexed cover W_i(t)=A_i when t∈J_i, and ∅ otherwise. Its members have diameter≤δ and their s-costs are bounded by ofReal(ρ_i^s)1_{J_i}(t). The definition of C_s therefore gives
16:     c:=C_s(δ,A) ≤ Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s)1_{J_i}(t)  for every t∈I.
17: Outside I use zero on both sides by multiplying every indicator by 1_I. Thus on all ℝ,
18:     c1_I ≤ Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s)1_{J_i∩I}.
19: All functions on the right are measurable, since J_i∩I is a Borel set, and all weights are finite nonnegative real powers. The same applies to the left even when c=∞. Apply B008 to this pointwise inequality, B006 to the nonnegative series with Lebesgue measure on ℝ, and B007 to each measurable indicator. Since volume(I)=1 by B009 and volume(J_i∩I)≤volume(J_i) by measure monotonicity, the result is
20:     c = c·1 ≤ Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s) volume(J_i∩I)
21:       ≤ Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^s) ofReal ρ_i
22:        = Σ_i ofReal(ρ_i^(s+1)).
23: The power identity holds for ρ_i>0 by real powers and for ρ_i=0 because both s and s+1 are positive. For empty indices both sides of the summand are zero. Measure monotonicity applies to every set and needs no additional regularity. All displayed operations are in [0,∞], where multiplication of these finite weights is well-defined, including the zero weights; no subtraction of infinities occurs. In particular no finiteness of c is needed.
24: 
25: This proves c≤cost(V) for every δ-cover. Taking the infimum over V yields C_s(δ,A)≤C_{s+1}(δ,A×I). Taking the supremum over finite positive δ, B101 gives H^s(A)≤H^(s+1)(A×I). This proves B102. The exact inequality has constant one in the maximum product metric, with no compactness assumption.
26: 
27: §3. Derivation of B103 (upper cover).
28: Suppose q>0 and H^q(A)=0. Fix a target scale δ>0 and an arbitrary ε>0. Apply B101 with r=min(1,δ)>0 to obtain U_i covering A and budgets 0<a_i≤r, with ediam U_i≤ofReal a_i and Σ a_i^q<ε in the extended-nonnegative interpretation. Define the integer N_i=ceil(1/a_i). Because 0<a_i≤1, N_i≥1, 1/N_i≤a_i, and
29:     N_i≤1/a_i+1≤2/a_i.
30: Cover I by the N_i closed intervals J_ij=[j/N_i,(j+1)/N_i], 0≤j<N_i. For every U_i and each such interval, distances between two points of U_i×J_ij are at most max(a_i,1/N_i)≤a_i. Hence its diameter in the maximum metric is at most a_i≤δ. The products cover A×I, and their indexing set {(i,j):i∈ℕ,0≤j<N_i} is countable: it injects into ℕ×ℕ, which is enumerated by successive finite diagonals. Reindex as a sequence, padding by empty sets if needed; the sum of nonnegative costs is unchanged. Their total (q+1)-cost is bounded by
31:     Σ_i N_i a_i^(q+1) ≤ Σ_i (2/a_i)a_i^(q+1)
32:       =2 Σ_i a_i^q <2ε.
33: The only division is by positive a_i, and the power identity is valid for every real q>0. This bound holds for every ε>0 at fixed δ, so the content C_{q+1}(δ,A×I)=0. B101 now gives H^(q+1)(A×I)=0. This proves B103 with the absolute factor 2; it does not depend on dimension or any choice of ambient box. Unlike the supplied upper argument, it applies without a separate n=0 branch.
34: 
35: §4. Derivation of B104 (nonempty slice).
36: If A is nonempty choose x₀∈A. For all t,u∈ℝ the maximum metric gives d((x₀,t),(x₀,u))=max(0,|t−u|)=|t−u|. Thus f(t)=(x₀,t) is 1-Lipschitz and 1-antilipschitz. B003 implies dimH(f(I))=dimH I=1, the last equality being B005. Since f(I)⊆A×I, dimension monotonicity gives dimH(A×I)≥1. To obtain that monotonicity from the precise bundled B003, instantiate B003 on the product space with its identity map and constants 1. This proves B104.
37: 
38: §5. Derivation of B105 (dimension equality in the maximum metric).
39: Let A be nonempty with finite Hausdorff dimension D. Regard D as a finite nonnegative real number; coercing it back to [0,∞] recovers dimH A. Put F=A×I. For every real q>D we have q>0. B002 gives H^q(A)=0. B103 gives H^(q+1)(F)=0, and B002 gives dimH F≤q+1 because zero is not infinity. This also proves dimH F is finite by taking, for example, q=D+1. Letting q decrease to D gives dimH F≤D+1: explicitly if the finite real number dimH F were >D+1, take q=D+(dimH F−D−1)/2, which contradicts dimH F≤q+1.
40: 
41: For the reverse direction, B104 gives dimH F≥1. If D=0 this is already ≥D+1. If D>0, fix any 0<s<D. B002 gives H^s(A)=∞. B102 gives H^(s+1)(F)=∞, and B002 then gives dimH F≥s+1. If dimH F<D+1, choose a positive s with max(0,dimH F−1)<s<D, possible since D>0 and dimH F−1<D. Then dimH F<s+1, contradiction. Thus dimH F≥D+1 in every case. This proves B105 with precisely the finite-D hypothesis, and without assuming D>0.
42: 
43: §6. Derivation of B106 (Euclidean metric bridge).
44: Use the object appendCoord n defined in lean_header: appendCoord n (x,t) has first n coordinates x_i and last coordinate t. Every y∈Ambient(n+1) has unique preimage (x,t) where x_i=y_i at the first n coordinates and t=y_last. The function Fin.lastCases in the definition implements exactly this coordinate splitting. For p=(x,t), p′=(x′,t′), put a=‖x−x′‖₂≥0 and b=|t−t′|≥0. Splitting the finite sum of squares of the n+1 coordinate differences gives
45:     d₂(appendCoord n p,appendCoord n p′)^2
46:        = Σ_{i<n}|x_i−x′_i|²+|t−t′|²=a²+b².
47: Since max(a,b)²≤a²+b²≤2max(a,b)², taking nonnegative square roots gives
48:     d_max(p,p′)≤d₂(appendCoord n p,appendCoord n p′)
49:        ≤√2 d_max(p,p′).
50: Thus appendCoord n is √2-Lipschitz and 1-antilipschitz, with constants independent of n and of E. B003 applied with K=√2 (as a nonnegative real), L=1 shows dimH(appendCoord n '' S)=dimH S for every subset S of the maximum-metric product. The argument includes n=0: the empty coordinate sum equals zero, x is the unique point of Ambient 0, and the last coordinate remains unchanged. No appeal to an unspecified norm-invariance theorem is needed.

52: §7. Original target and replacement account.
53: Return to the original arbitrary n∈ℕ and original nonempty compact E⊆Ambient n. By B004, dimH E≤n and is finite, even for n=0. Its image under coordinate concatenation is precisely the original subset E×[0,1] of Euclidean ℝ^(n+1). Thus its Euclidean Hausdorff dimension is dimH E+1, as required. All original H are retained, with compactness explicitly unused in this strengthened route. There is no specified algorithm in this task to preserve.

value.full_target:
Here dimension means **Hausdorff dimension**. As approved by the user on
2026-10-23, assume explicitly that \(E\) is nonempty. With the convention
\(\dim_H\varnothing=0\), the printed equality would otherwise fail for
the empty set. This is a disclosed addition to the printed exercise.

Let \(n\geq0\) be an integer, let \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty
compact set, and put \(I=[0,1]\). Identify \(\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R\)
with \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\) and use its Euclidean metric. Prove

\[
\dim_H(E\times[0,1])=\dim_H E+1.
\]

The zero-dimensional ambient space \(\mathbb R^0\) is included. A later
formalization using a different product norm must justify the metric change.
value.conclusion: With the stipulated Euclidean metrics and identification ℝ^n×ℝ=ℝ^(n+1), dimH(E×[0,1])=dimH(E)+1; equivalently dimH(appendCoord(n) '' (E×I))=dimH(E)+1. Both dimensions are finite, so this is also the equality of their real values.

definitions.type: ℕ → real finite dimensional inner product spaces
definitions.definition: Ambient(m)=EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin m), the space of m real coordinates with norm ‖x‖₂=(Σ_{j<m}|x_j|²)^(1/2). The sum is zero when m=0. Distances are norms of differences. More generally the native EuclideanSpace k (Fin m), for a real-or-complex-like field k, is the m-coordinate k-space with this same sum-of-squared-absolute-values norm; its scalar vector-space structure is coordinatewise.

binders.type: vector in the indicated real or k-valued coordinate space

definitions.type: extended diameter of a subset of any pseudo extended metric space
definitions.definition: For a pseudo extended metric space Z and B⊆Z, ediam(B)=sup{edist(x,y):x∈B,y∈B} in [0,∞], with supremum of the empty set zero. For finite ediam, diam(B)=(ediam B).toReal and ediam B=ofReal(diam B). In metric spaces edist is ofReal of the ordinary distance.
ofReal(v) is max(v,0) embedded in the extended nonnegative reals. The notation z.toReal for z∈[0,∞] is its real value when finite, and zero for z=∞.

definitions.type: real exponent × extended scale × subset of an extended metric space → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: For an extended metric space Z, exponent u∈ℝ, scale h∈[0,∞], and B⊆Z, Content(u,h,B)=inf_{U:ℕ→Set Z; B⊆⋃_i U_i; ∀i ediam(U_i)≤h} Σ_i sup_{(_ : U_i nonempty)} (ediam U_i)^u. Infima, suprema and sums are in [0,∞]; an infimum over no covers is ∞. This is exactly the Content in basis-registry.json /lean_header. Countable covers may be padded by empty sets.

definitions.type: real exponent × real scale × subset → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: C_u(h,B), also written C_u(h,B), means Content(u,ofReal h,B) for real scale h. We use it only at h>0.

binders.type: subset of an extended metric space

definitions.type: real exponent × subset of a Borel extended metric space → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: H^u(B)=μH[u](B) denotes Mathlib's unnormalized Hausdorff measure, the metric measure mkMetric for the gauge r↦r^u on the Borel sigma algebra. The metric-measure construction takes countable-cover outer contents for this gauge, with the empty-set gauge cost forced to zero, and their supremum as the scale tends to zero. Its precise cover evaluation will be applied as an explicit native source, rather than assumed as an extra premise. No spherical or dimensional normalization factor is used.

binders.type: subset of a Borel extended metric space

definitions.type: subset of an extended metric space → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: For B in an extended metric space, equipped with its Borel measurable structure when computing H, dimH(B)=sup{d∈[0,∞): H^d(B)=∞}, the supremum taken in [0,∞] and with sup ∅=0. This is native Mathlib dimH. Positive-exponent critical-exponent directions are invoked as explicit native sources. We use no zero-exponent measure assertion.

binders.type: subset of an extended metric space

definitions.type: subset of ℝ
definitions.definition: I=[0,1]={t∈ℝ:0≤t≤1}. This is unitInterval in the basis header.

definitions.type: metric space → metric spaces
definitions.definition: For a metric space Z, MaxProd(Z)=Z×ℝ with distance d_max((x,t),(y,u))=max(d_Z(x,y),|t−u|). For B⊆Z, B×I always denotes a subset of MaxProd(Z) in intermediate lemmas. All metric spaces in integration or Hausdorff-measure statements carry their Borel sigma algebra.

definitions.type: for m∈ℕ, MaxProd(Ambient m) → Ambient(m+1)
definitions.definition: appendCoord(m)(x,t) is the vector whose first m coordinates are those of x and whose last coordinate is t. In the exact basis header it is WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.lastCases t (fun j => x j)). Its target always carries the Euclidean norm; its source here carries the maximum metric. It is a total coordinate construction, including m=0. Under the problem's identification ℝ^n×ℝ=ℝ^(n+1), the Euclidean set E×[0,1] is appendCoord(n) '' (E×I).

definitions.type: measure on the Borel sets of ℝ
definitions.definition: volume is Lebesgue measure on ℝ, with its usual Borel measurable structure (and its extension as an outer measure on arbitrary sets). Thus measure monotonicity applies to all subsets; no measurability of a covering set is implicit.

definitions.type: subset × constant → functions
definitions.definition: For a set B⊆Z and a scalar c∈[0,∞], c1_B denotes the function equal to c on B and zero off B, that is B.indicator(fun _ => c). This is meaningful for c=∞ as well, with no subtraction of infinities.

definitions.type: measure × nonnegative extended function → [0,∞]
definitions.definition: For a measurable space Z, measure μ and f:Z→[0,∞], ∫⁻ f dμ (the lower Lebesgue integral, lintegral) is the supremum of ∫g dμ over measurable nonnegative simple functions g≤f; a simple function integral is its finite sum of values times the measures of the corresponding disjoint level sets. All integrals in the slicing proof are lower integrals; integrability is never required.

binders.type: nonnegative measurable simple function on Z

definitions.type: nonnegative real × map of pseudo extended metric spaces → propositions
definitions.definition: LipschitzWith(K,f) means ∀x,y, edist(f x,f y)≤K·edist(x,y), where K is a finite nonnegative real embedded into [0,∞]. On metric spaces this is the usual distance inequality.

binders.type: map between pseudo extended metric spaces

definitions.type: nonnegative real × map of extended metric spaces → propositions
definitions.definition: AntilipschitzWith(L,f) means ∀x,y, edist(x,y)≤L·edist(f x,f y), with finite L≥0. On metric spaces this is the corresponding ordinary distance inequality.

definitions.type: ordered field or real vector space × endpoints → subsets
definitions.definition: segment(k,x,y)={a•x+b•y: a,b∈k, a≥0,b≥0,a+b=1}, in a vector space over an ordered scalar field k; over ℝ this is the usual closed line segment.

definitions.type: field × vector space → ℕ
definitions.definition: finrank(k,Z) is the dimension as a natural number of a finite-dimensional k-vector space Z (and is zero by the native total convention if the vector-space rank is infinite). In this proof its arguments are finite dimensional.

definitions.type: real or extended nonnegative base × real exponent → corresponding scalars
definitions.definition: The notation v^u uses the standard real power; on positive real v it is exp(u log v), with 0^u=0 for u>0 and 0^0=1. For extended nonnegative bases it is the usual extension: at u>0, ∞^u=∞ and 0^u=0; at u=0 the value is 1; at u<0, 0^u=∞ and ∞^u=0. Only nonnegative real bases and positive exponents occur in the covering calculations. The native real function at negative v is defined using |v|, as in Real.rpow.

value.representation_notes: Keep the exact prepared YuiBasis header as prefix. Ambient n is EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n): Fin n is the coordinate index type, and EuclideanSpace is PiLp 2, so 2 is the norm exponent, not a dimension parameter. Native X×ℝ has the maximum metric (Prod.dist_eq); set products are Set.prod (×ˢ). appendCoord uses Fin.lastCases to put t at Fin.last n and x_i at i.castSucc, with WithLp.toLp 2 selecting the target Euclidean norm. T012/T013 prove the actual metric conversion. H s A is the native unnormalized hausdorffMeasure on the canonical Borel sigma algebra of each metric space, with the BorelSpace equality witnessed definitionally; it adds no regularity assumption. C s δ A is exactly prepared Content s (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A. ENNReal.ofReal embeds max(δ,0), and only positive real scales occur in content assertions. Metric.ediam, infima, suprema, sums, dimensions and costs take values in ℝ≥0∞, retaining ∞; ^ on extended diameters is ENNReal real power, while ^ on real budgets is Real.rpow before ofReal. Positive exponents make empty costs zero. dimH uses Borel Hausdorff measure and nonnegative critical exponents intrinsically. Finite-dimensional and finite-product results imply that the final ENNReal equality is also equality of real dimensions. All H premises and N/P outputs are kept; no E exists here, no M port is needed, and reviewed background notes introduce no assumptions.

R004.fact: For every natural n, the real coordinate space Ambient n with its given Euclidean inner product and norm is a finite-dimensional real normed vector space. Its coordinate vectors e_j, j∈Fin n, form a basis, including the empty basis for n=0; its metric also supplies an extended metric.

grounds.reason: n is a natural number, including zero, so Fin n is finite.
Ambient n is the real coordinate space with coordinatewise vector operations and its Euclidean inner product/norm.

R004.justification: Define e_j to have coordinate 1 at j and 0 elsewhere. Each x equals the finite sum Σ_j x_j e_j by evaluation at each coordinate. If Σ_j a_j e_j=0, evaluation at j gives a_j=0, proving independence. For n=0 every vector is the unique empty tuple, and spanning and independence hold for the empty family. Hence the space is finite dimensional. The supplied Euclidean inner product induces the displayed norm and the compatible real normed-space structure. Regard each finite real distance as an extended nonnegative distance to obtain the extended metric, preserving the metric axioms.

R005.fact: The real numbers with norm |x| and their usual addition and real scalar multiplication form a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, of dimension one, with basis consisting of 1.

grounds.reason: S001 explicitly takes the ambient space to be ℝ, with the standard real normed-space interpretation.
The supplied M012 statement requires the ambient real normed space to be finite dimensional; the present routine verification supplies precisely this condition for ℝ.

R005.justification: The real field operations give the real vector-space and additive-group laws. Absolute value is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at zero, is subadditive, and satisfies |a x|=|a||x|, so it gives the stated compatible norm. Every real x equals x·1, and a·1=0 implies a=0. Thus the singleton 1 spans and is linearly independent, proving finite dimensionality.

R101.fact: For the D004 infimum, enlarging the allowed scale decreases Content. Its supremum over positive extended scales equals its supremum over scales ofReal δ with real δ>0.

grounds.reason: Admissibility is the diameter upper bound; the value is an infimum in [0,∞].
The proof gives a positive finite δ with ofReal δ≤h for every positive extended h.

R101.justification: Every cover allowed at a smaller scale is allowed at a larger scale, so the larger-scale infimum is no greater. Each positive real scale occurs among the extended scales. Conversely each extended-scale content is bounded above by the content at the displayed smaller positive real scale. Taking suprema gives both inequalities.

R101.fact: If an infimum of admissible cover costs in [0,∞] equals zero, then for every real t>0 an admissible cover has cost <ofReal t.

grounds.reason: F001 expresses H as a supremum of nonnegative real-scale contents.
L2 gives H=0 and r,ε>0; hence the content at r/2 is zero and t=ε/4 is positive.

R101.justification: Each content is bounded above by the zero supremum and below by zero. If no admissible cost were below ofReal t, that positive number would be a lower bound for all costs, contradicting infimum zero. The empty family has infimum ∞, so cannot be the family here.

R101.fact: If z≤ofReal(r/2) with real r>0, then z is finite, d=z.toReal satisfies 0≤d≤r/2 and z=ofReal d. For s>0, (ofReal d)^s=ofReal(d^s).

grounds.reason: D002 supplies finite-diameter conversion.
D003 defines the finite embedding and toReal.
D018 specifies the corresponding real and extended powers.
F002 bounds every diameter by ofReal(r/2).

R101.justification: The upper bound is finite, so toReal is the inverse order-preserving real coordinate and gives the stated bounds. At d=0 both powers are zero since s>0. At d>0 both use the same positive real power, and the embedding preserves its value. This verifies the termwise cost conversion.

R101.fact: For ε>0 and e_i=ε·2^(−i−3), each e_i>0 and the real and extended nonnegative sums equal ε/4 and ofReal(ε/4), respectively.

grounds.reason: L2 gives ε>0.
S003 defines e and displays its finite partial sum (ε/4)(1−2^(−m)).

R101.justification: The displayed finite geometric identity follows by multiplying the partial sum by 1−1/2. The sequence 2^(−m) tends to zero (for example 2^m≥m+1 gives the elementary reciprocal bound). Thus the nonnegative partial sums increase to ε/4. Their supremum is the extended nonnegative sum, yielding the same finite embedded value.

R101.fact: For every i, continuity of x↦x^s at d_i, e_i>0 and d_i<r yield a_i with d_i<a_i<r and a_i^s<d_i^s+e_i; these choices may be made as a sequence.

grounds.reason: M020 supplies continuity once s≥0.
L1 gives s>0.
F003 supplies the real d_i, e_i>0, and d_i<r.

R101.justification: Continuity gives a radius ρ_i>0 for error e_i. Take η_i=(1/2)min(ρ_i,r−d_i)>0. Then η_i<ρ_i and η_i<r−d_i, so a_i=d_i+η_i has the claimed interval and power bounds. Ordinary countable choice of the established nonempty radius choices produces the sequence, as explicitly used in S004; no uniform radius or enlarged covering set is needed.

R101.fact: For nonnegative real sequences b_i,c_i,f_i with f_i≤b_i+c_i and finite totals B=Σ_i ofReal b_i, C=Σ_i ofReal c_i, one has Σ_i ofReal f_i≤B+C. In this application B<ofReal(ε/4), C=ofReal(ε/4), hence the budget total is <ofReal ε.

grounds.reason: F003 gives nonnegative d_i, positive errors, the bound on the original total and the finite error total.
F004 gives positive a_i and a_i^s<d_i^s+e_i.
s>0 ensures all these real powers are nonnegative.

R101.justification: For every finite initial segment, monotonicity and finite addition give the corresponding sum bound. Nonnegative series are suprema of these partial sums. The partial sums of b and c increase to their finite totals, so their sums increase to B+C; taking suprema proves the claimed weak bound. With b_i=d_i^s, c_i=e_i and f_i=a_i^s, finite scalar addition and ε>0 give B+C<ofReal(ε/2)<ofReal ε. No interchange involving signed terms or infinite strict addition is used.

R102.fact: If d is an extended nonnegative real, delta is a finite nonnegative real and d<=ofReal(delta), then d is finite, 0<=d.toReal<=delta and ofReal(d.toReal)=d. For finite nonnegative reals a,b, ofReal(a)<=ofReal(b) is equivalent to a<=b.

grounds.reason: L1 gives delta>0 and L2 bounds each d=ediam(V_i) by ofReal(delta).
D003 identifies finite extended nonnegative values with their real values.

R102.justification: The finite bound excludes the top element. The order-preserving identification of the finite nonnegative part with the nonnegative real half-line gives the two inequalities and inverse conversion. This also permits passing from a pointwise edist bound to the real absolute-distance bound used in S002.

R102.fact: The real numbers with their usual order and metric bornology form an order bornology: metric-bounded sets are order-bounded, and every interval with finite real endpoints is metric-bounded. Thus the real structure satisfies the structural order/bornology premise of M018.

grounds.reason: M018 requires a conditionally complete lattice with compatible bornology.
Each Bproj_i is contained in a finite interval in its nonempty branch.

R102.justification: A real set lying in a ball of radius R about a lies in [a-R,a+R]. Conversely a set contained between real bounds p,q has distances from p bounded by max(q-p,0). The usual real order is conditionally complete. These facts identify the order and metric boundedness structures used in the stated application.

R102.fact: For arbitrary finite real endpoints a,b the interval [a,b] is closed, hence Borel measurable, also when empty. The empty set and finite intersections of such sets are Borel measurable.

grounds.reason: J_i is either empty or a closed real interval; I=[0,1].
D008 defines I.
D011 fixes the Borel measurable structure on R.

R102.justification: The complement of [a,b] is the union of the open rays (-infinity,a) and (b,infinity). Closed sets are complements of open sets and belong to the Borel sigma algebra, which is closed under finite intersections.

R102.fact: For u>0, the map d -> d^u is increasing on extended nonnegative reals. For finite r>=0, (ofReal(r))^u=ofReal(r^u); also (ofReal(r^u))*ofReal(r)=ofReal(r^(u+1)).

grounds.reason: F001 gives finite 0<=rho_i<=delta and the projection diameter bounds.
L1 gives s>0, hence s+1>0.
D018 supplies the standard power conventions.

R102.justification: On positive finite bases, monotonicity follows from increasing log and exp and multiplication by u>0. The identity r^u*r=r^(u+1) follows by adding exponents in exp(u log r). At r=0 both positive powers vanish, and the extended endpoints follow from 0^u=0 and infinity^u=infinity. Embedding finite nonnegative reals preserves products and the defined powers. import Mathlib
open scoped ENNReal NNReal Topology
open MeasureTheory MeasureTheory.Measure Set Metric
namespace YuiBasis
noncomputable def Content {X : Type*} [EMetricSpace X]
    (s : ℝ) (δ : ℝ≥0∞) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  ⨅ (U : ℕ → Set X) (_ : A ⊆ ⋃ i, U i) (_ : ∀ i, Metric.ediam (U i) ≤ δ),
    ∑' i, ⨆ (_ : (U i).Nonempty), Metric.ediam (U i) ^ s
abbrev Ambient (n : ℕ) := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin n)
def unitInterval : Set ℝ := Set.Icc 0 1
noncomputable def appendCoord (n : ℕ) (p : Ambient n × ℝ) : Ambient (n + 1) :=
  WithLp.toLp 2 (Fin.lastCases p.2 (fun i => p.1 i))
end YuiBasis

open YuiBasis
namespace YuiPlan
noncomputable def H {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (s : ℝ) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  letI : MeasurableSpace X := borel X
  letI : BorelSpace X := ⟨rfl⟩
  hausdorffMeasure s A
noncomputable def C {X : Type*} [MetricSpace X] (s δ : ℝ) (A : Set X) : ℝ≥0∞ :=
  YuiBasis.Content s (ENNReal.ofReal δ) A
end YuiPlan
open YuiPlan

R004.fact: For every natural n, the real coordinate space Ambient n with its given Euclidean inner product and norm is a finite-dimensional real normed vector space. Its coordinate vectors e_j, j∈Fin n, form a basis, including the empty basis for n=0; its metric also supplies an extended metric.

grounds.reason: n is a natural number, including zero, so Fin n is finite.
Ambient n is the real coordinate space with coordinatewise vector operations and its Euclidean inner product/norm.

R004.justification: Define e_j to have coordinate 1 at j and 0 elsewhere. Each x equals the finite sum Σ_j x_j e_j by evaluation at each coordinate. If Σ_j a_j e_j=0, evaluation at j gives a_j=0, proving independence. For n=0 every vector is the unique empty tuple, and spanning and independence hold for the empty family. Hence the space is finite dimensional. The supplied Euclidean inner product induces the displayed norm and the compatible real normed-space structure. Regard each finite real distance as an extended nonnegative distance to obtain the extended metric, preserving the metric axioms.

R005.fact: The real numbers with norm |x| and their usual addition and real scalar multiplication form a finite-dimensional real normed vector space, of dimension one, with basis consisting of 1.

grounds.reason: S001 explicitly takes the ambient space to be ℝ, with the standard real normed-space interpretation.
The supplied M012 statement requires the ambient real normed space to be finite dimensional; the present routine verification supplies precisely this condition for ℝ.

R005.justification: The real field operations give the real vector-space and additive-group laws. Absolute value is nonnegative, vanishes exactly at zero, is subadditive, and satisfies |a x|=|a||x|, so it gives the stated compatible norm. Every real x equals x·1, and a·1=0 implies a=0. Thus the singleton 1 spans and is linearly independent, proving finite dimensionality.

R101.fact: For the D004 infimum, enlarging the allowed scale decreases Content. Its supremum over positive extended scales equals its supremum over scales ofReal δ with real δ>0.

value.N005: dimH(I)=1 in the usual real metric.
value.N101: For every metric space X, subset A⊆X and real s>0: C_s(δ,A) at every real δ>0 is the infimum of Σ_i(ediam U_i)^s over natural-indexed δ-covers of A, empty members contributing zero. If 0<δ₁≤δ₂ then C_s(δ₂,A)≤C_s(δ₁,A). Moreover H^s(A)=sup_{δ∈ℝ,δ>0} C_s(δ,A), so H agrees exactly with the unnormalized positive-exponent Hausdorff measure of problem.md. If H^s(A)=0, then for every r>0 and ε>0 there exist a natural-indexed cover U of A and real budgets a:ℕ→ℝ such that 0<a_i≤r, ediam U_i≤ofReal(a_i), and Σ_i ofReal(a_i^s)<ofReal ε.
value.N102: For every metric space X, subset A⊆X, real s>0 and finite real δ>0, C_s(δ,A)≤C_{s+1}(δ,A×I) in the maximum product metric MaxProd(X). Consequently H^s(A)≤H^{s+1}(A×I), including infinite values. The slicing constant is exactly one; neither compactness nor measurability of A or its covers is required.
value.N103: For every metric space X, A⊆X and real q>0, H^q(A)=0 implies H^{q+1}(A×I)=0 in MaxProd X. Under the same hypotheses q>0 and H^q(A)=0, for every target scale δ>0 and tolerance ε>0 there exists a natural-indexed cover of A×I whose members have extended diameter≤ofReal δ and whose total (q+1)-cost is <ofReal(2ε). The constant 2 is absolute, independent of X,A,δ,q.
value.N104: For every metric space X and nonempty A⊆X, dimH(A×I)≥1 in the maximum metric MaxProd X.
value.N105: For every metric space X and nonempty A⊆X with dimH(A)≠∞, the maximum product metric satisfies dimH(A×I)=dimH(A)+1 in [0,∞], and dimH(A×I)≠∞. Thus the corresponding finite real dimensions satisfy the same equality. No compactness or positive-dimension assumption is required.
value.N106: The map appendCoord(n):MaxProd(Ambient n)→Ambient(n+1) is bijective and, for all p,p′ in its source, d_max(p,p′)≤d₂(appendCoord(n)p,appendCoord(n)p′)≤√2·d_max(p,p′). Thus it is √2-Lipschitz and 1-antilipschitz, and for every subset S⊆MaxProd(Ambient n), dimH(appendCoord(n) '' S)=dimH(S). Constants are independent of n and E. This includes n=0.
value.P: With the stipulated Euclidean metrics and identification ℝ^n×ℝ=ℝ^(n+1), dimH(E×[0,1])=dimH(E)+1; equivalently dimH(appendCoord(n) '' (E×I))=dimH(E)+1. Both dimensions are finite, so this is also the equality of their real values.

argument.text: Ambient n is the n-coordinate real inner product space, hence a finite-dimensional real normed vector space: its n coordinate vectors span and are independent, also for the empty coordinate family at n=0. Apply M008 to E⊆univ, M009 to this whole space, and M011 with scalar field ℝ and natural index n. This gives dimH E≤dimH(univ:Ambient n)=finrank(ℝ,Ambient n)=n. Nonnegativity is part of the [0,∞] codomain of dimH. M010 applied to E in the same space gives dimH E≠∞. No compactness or nonemptiness is used.
